## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run yet. In the earlier search, 84 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success, so no idea has any evidence behind it yet. Both scores being 0 means the agent never finishes an exact build. That makes optimisation and inductive bias the priorities, not generalisation. The starting net's footprint pooling can in principle express 'all covered cells are at the same height and the next missing cell is there'. It still fails, so I suspect optimisation, initialisation or the recipe, or footprint alignment that is off in this changed world. This round goes for breadth. Each candidate stacks the untested ideas: orthogonal init, near-uniform starting logits (gain 0.01), GroupNorm, a learned skip carrying raw obs into the head, and factorised type/anchor/interaction logits. On top of that, each one changes something different: a dense or learned footprint-shaped conv head, a deep per-cell MLP, dilation, and recipe extremes (lr 3e-3, clip 0.3, long rollouts with 1 epoch, small minibatches, large batches with low gamma).

### Round 2
Round 1 looks like the 84 earlier trials. All six candidates scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success. They tried orthogonal init with small logit gain, GroupNorm, a raw-obs skip, factorised logits, footprint-conv heads, and recipe extremes from lr 3e-3 with 1 epoch to 4096-sample batches. The agent never finishes an exact build, even in training, so we still have no evidence for any idea. Every round-1 head was anchored at the top-left. If this world's anchor convention or landing rule differs, those heads may be misaligned. The trunks were also local, with at most about a 7x7 receptive field. This round tries new structural biases, each stacked with init hygiene: centred wide-kernel heads that work under any anchor offset, a U-Net for whole-board context, weight-tied recurrent convs, a learned conv along the layer axis (surface and overhang structure), and the legality mask as learned input planes. Recipes also vary widely. Nothing has scored above 0, so I'm not ablating yet.

### Round 3
After 18 trials, one has a real signal. r2c1 scored 0.0605 on dev and 0.0199 on training success. It uses a centred 5x5 per-type output conv on a 3-block GroupNorm residual trunk, with coordinate channels, attention pooling and 2 epochs at gamma 0.99 and lambda 0.95. Every other trial scored 0, except r2c3 at 0.002, which is noise-level. Other centred-head nets (U-Net, weight-tied trunk, layer-axis stem, the "everything" stack) still scored 0. So the centred head may be necessary but is not sufficient, or r2c1 was a lucky seed. Every top-left-anchored head has failed, which hints that the world's anchor convention or landing offset differs from the description. Training success is above 0, so the agent can now finish exact builds. This round stays near r2c1, following step 6 of the program:
- one near-copy at a different width;
- four single-change variants (more fresh samples, lower entropy, a raw-obs skip into the head, a deeper trunk);
- one stack of compatible changes.

### Round 4
Only the centred-head GroupNorm residual family (r2c1) has learned. Its width-32 copy r3c1 (r≈1, 242k steps) reached 11.1% dev and 9.7% train success. r2c1 itself scored 6%. All changes that added compute or sharpened the policy did worse: the raw-obs skip (0.4%), a deeper trunk (0.2%), lower entropy (0.2%) and the stack (3.1%). Switching to 1 epoch with 32-step rollouts scored 0. Training and dev success are similar, so the problem is optimisation and sample efficiency, not generalisation. Because r is already about 1, shrinking the net further gives no extra steps. The only levers left are the recipe and the noise between seeds. This is the last round, so I am spending it on single-change recipe variants of r3c1. The most promising are higher entropy (lower entropy hurt), more minibatches, 3 epochs, a higher learning rate, longer rollouts and a longer horizon for the +1 exact-build bonus. Each variant also re-tests whether r3c1's result holds up under a slightly different setup.
